answers.text: A polynomial-time decider can act as a verifier that ignores the certificate.
answers.explanation: For a problem in P, run its deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. It accepts exactly the yes-instances, regardless of the supplied certificate.

answers.text: NP means problems outside polynomial time.
answers.explanation: NP means nondeterministic polynomial time; it does not exclude P.

answers.text: Every problem can be solved in polynomial time.
answers.explanation: This is false; decidable problems exist outside P.

answers.text: All NP problems are already known to be in P.
answers.explanation: Whether P equals NP is unresolved.

answers.text: A verifier is allowed exponential time.
answers.explanation: An NP verifier must run in polynomial time.
P includes decision problems with both yes- and no-instances.

answers.text: The certificate may contain an arbitrarily long computation.
answers.explanation: NP certificates must have polynomial length.

answers.text: The verifier can accept without inspecting the input.
answers.explanation: It must still distinguish yes- and no-instances; running the decider does that.
Membership in P does not imply NP-hardness.

answers.text: Deterministic and nondeterministic polynomial time are proven equal.
answers.explanation: Only containment is known in general; equality is an open question.
